title: Tagore's Gitanjali (public domain, 1912)
hook: a poet tells a worshiper to open the temple doors and look outside

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tagore's Gitanjali opened at its first poem: the frail vessel emptied and filled, the little reed flute, and still room to fill.

A dark corner of a temple. The doors are shut. Someone sits there with a string of beads, chanting, eyes closed. It's a real and honored form of devotion. And in one Gitanjali poem, the poet walks up to that person and says, in effect: stop. Open your eyes. Your God isn't before you. Today, poem eleven, and where Tagore says to look instead.
screen: `A DARK CORNER, DOORS SHUT.` → `OPEN YOUR EYES.` → `WHERE TO LOOK INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Here are the opening lines, in Tagore's own English: "Leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! Whom dost thou worship in this lonely dark corner of a temple with doors all shut? Open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee!" Then he says where God is: "He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground and where the pathmaker is breaking stones." God is with them in sun and in shower, the poem says, his garment covered in dust, and it tells the worshiper to put off the holy mantle and come down onto the dusty soil too. The poem doesn't sneer at the worshiper. But it does say plainly: leave the beads, and later, the flowers and incense too. Its sharpest picture is the shut doors: a devotion walled off from people working in the sun misses where God already is. Tagore's family belonged to the Brahmo Samaj, a reform movement wary of image worship, and the poem carries that voice. Hindus who pray with beads and flowers may answer that their worship is where they learn to see God in the field. The worshiper hopes for deliverance, freedom from all this. Where is such deliverance to be found, the poem asks, since the master himself has joyfully taken on the bonds of creation? God isn't escaping the world. God is bound up in it, on purpose, gladly. The poem closes by telling the worshiper to meet him and stand by him in toil and in the sweat of the brow. The place of worship and the place of work turn out to be the same place.
screen: `LEAVE THE CHANTING, OPEN YOUR EYES.` · `GOD IS WITH THE TILLER AND THE PATHMAKER.` · `THE COMPLAINT IS THE SHUT DOOR.` · `GOD HAS TAKEN ON THE BONDS OF CREATION.` · then, large: `MEET HIM IN TOIL.`

segments.voice: Open your eyes and let your gaze rest on what's in front of you. Bring to mind someone whose work you depend on and rarely see, whoever grew today's food, laid the road outside or cleans the building, and stay with one of them, at work in sun or rain. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, right where they're working; if not, simply keep them in view, with some gratitude.
Tagore's Gitanjali. In poem eleven, the doors come open, and God is found where the tiller tills and the pathmaker breaks stones.
Your line: God with the tiller. Tomorrow, a poem built on one small word. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Hindus pray in many ways, with beads and chanting in a temple corner as well as through daily work, and Tagore's poem is one poet's voice within the tradition, often read as a call to find God among working people.
